chunks: From him, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Sama'ah, from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Tatari, who said:

The matter upon which there is consensus regarding divorce is that he says to her, 'You are divorced,' or 'Observe the waiting period.' It was narrated that he said to Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, 'How do you bear witness to his saying, 'Observe the waiting period'?' He said, 'He says, 'Bear witness that I have divorced you (or: Observe the waiting period).' ' Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah said, 'This is an error. Divorce is not except as Bukayr ibn A'yan narrated: He says to her while she is pure from non-coitus, 'You are divorced,' and he calls two just witnesses. And everything other than that is void.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The hadiths that we have presented, from their saying 'Observe the waiting period,' can be interpreted in a way that does not contradict the sound ruling according to what Ibn Sama'ah said, because their saying 'Observe the waiting period' only serves as consideration (or: is effective) if preceded by the man's saying 'You are divorced,' then he says 'Observe the waiting period,' because his saying to her 'Observe the waiting period' does not have a meaning in itself, because she could say, 'From what [cause] do I observe the waiting period?' Therefore, he must say to her, 'Observe the waiting period, for I have divorced you.' Thus, the consideration is with the divorce, not with this saying, except that this saying serves as a clarifier for her that the ruling of divorce has become binding upon her and necessitates that for her. And if it were isolated without the word of divorce preceding it, it would not be considered according to what Ibn Sama'ah said.
ai.seo_question: What are the essential conditions and phrasing for a valid divorce in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Istibsar clarifies the distinction between explicit (sarih) and metaphorical (kinayah) divorce formulas, emphasizing that 'observe the waiting period' (i'taddi) serves as a confirmatory indicator rather than the constitutive act itself. It highlights the scholarly debate regarding the necessity of witnesses and the specific condition of the wife being in a state of purity (taharah) without prior intercourse, reflecting the rigorous evidentiary standards in Shia fiqh. The text resolves apparent contradictions by interpreting 'i'taddi' as a declaration of the legal consequence rather than the divorce act itself, ensuring alignment with the consensus view.
